body.en:
• Java releases roughly every 6 months now; LTS versions (8, 11, 17, 21) are what industry standardises on.
  • Java 7: try-with-resources, strings in switch, diamond operator, multi-catch.
  • Java 8 (the revolution): lambda expressions, Stream API, java.time, default methods in interfaces.
  • Java 9-11: modules (JPMS), jshell, var for locals, HttpClient.
  • Java 14-17: switch expressions, text blocks, records, pattern-matching instanceof, sealed classes.
  • The diploma lab JDK is 11, so lambda/streams/var run here; the 14+ syntax appears as study-exhibits (jv5_12) and in exam theory.

• try-with-resources: declare an AutoCloseable object in the try header and the JVM closes it on EVERY exit path - the finally block of Unit 4 becomes unnecessary for pure cleanup.
  • Strings in switch: direct case labels like "Friday" - far clearer than an if-else ladder over equals().
  • Diamond operator: new ArrayList<>() reads the element type from the declaration on the left.
  • Multi-catch: catch (A | B e) - one recovery block for unrelated exception types.

jv5_1 closes a Scanner without finally; jv5_2 packs switch-on-String, diamond and multi-catch into one genuine run.

h.en: var, java.time and the Post-8 Wave

body.en:
• var (Java 10): local-variable type inference - javac copies the type from the right side; still fully static, not JavaScript-style dynamic typing.
  • Rules of var: locals and loops only; must be initialised where declared; not for fields, parameters or return types.
  • record (16+): one line declares an immutable data carrier with constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString.
  • Pattern-matching instanceof (16+): if (o instanceof String t) tests and binds in one step - no manual cast.
  • Also in the wave: text blocks (15+), sealed classes (17+), switch expressions (14+).
  • java.time (Java 8): LocalDate/LocalTime/Period - immutable, thread-safe, with clean formatting; it retired Date/Calendar for everyday work.

jv5_3 runs var on JDK 11; jv5_11 counts down to an exam date with java.time; jv5_12 shows records/patterns as commented exhibits beside their classic equivalents.

• A functional interface has EXACTLY ONE abstract method (any number of default/static ones) - that single method is what the lambda implements.
  • Lambda syntax: (parameters) -> body; empty parentheses when no parameters; a single expression needs no braces and no return keyword; braces for multi-statement bodies.
  • javac matches parameter types from the interface's method signature, so lambda parameter types are usually omitted.
  • @FunctionalInterface asks the compiler to police the one-method rule.

jv5_4 contrasts a 5-line anonymous class with its one-line lambda twin - both print, both are Speaker objects.

h.en: Lambdas with Parameters: Passing Behaviour Around

body.en:
• Calc add = (x, y) -> x + y; - one contract, many behaviours, each a two-word class.
  • Lambdas are values: store them in variables, pass them to methods, call them later - code becomes data.
  • This is run-time flexibility without inheritance: the strategy is chosen by which lambda you pass, not by which subclass you wrote.

jv5_5 passes add/sub/mul/div lambdas of the same Calc type into a shared show() method.

h.en: forEach and the Ready-made Functional Interfaces

body.en:
• Every collection owns forEach(Consumer): team.forEach(t -> println(...)) visits each element - the syllabus' "print list elements" task.
  • Meet the built-ins of java.util.function: Supplier<T> (get), Consumer<T> (accept), Predicate<T> (test), Function<T,R> (apply); plus old friend Runnable (run).
  • These five cover filter/map/forEach/factory tasks without writing your own interfaces.

jv5_6 prints a list three ways; jv5_10 runs Runnable and Supplier lambdas directly.

• A stream is a conveyor-belt view over a collection - not a container, not a loop.
  • filter(Predicate) keeps elements whose test is true; map(Function) transforms each element; forEach(Consumer) consumes them.
  • The source collection is never mutated - streams compute views; a spent stream cannot be reused.
  • Practical 15: filter even numbers (jv5_7) and map strings to uppercase (jv5_8) - exactly the two required tasks.

h.en: Full Pipelines: sorted, collect, and Laziness

body.en:
• Pipelines chain intermediate steps (filter, map, sorted - each returns a new stream) and end with ONE terminal step (forEach, count, collect).
  • Intermediate steps are lazy: nothing flows until the terminal step starts the belt - this enables wholesale optimisation.
  • collect(Collectors.toList()) pours the survivors back into a real modifiable List.
  • Style gain: whole "data questions" read as one readable sentence instead of nested loops with temp lists.

jv5_9 filters passes, sorts them, maps to grade strings and collects - one pipeline, new list, originals intact.

h.en: Meaning of AI and Machine Learning

body.en:
• Artificial Intelligence: the goal - getting machines to perform tasks that would need human intelligence (recognise, decide, predict, translate).
  • Machine Learning: the dominant approach inside AI - instead of hand-writing every rule, the program learns behaviour from data/examples. Change the data, and behaviour changes without rewriting code.
  • Deep Learning: ML using layered neural networks - today's image/speech/language breakthroughs.
  • Exam line: AI is the destination; ML is the road paved with examples; DL is the newest, fastest vehicle on that road.

h.en: Role of Java in AI and Its Libraries

body.en:
• Java dominates enterprise backends; AI columns inside such systems (fraud scores, recommendations, routing) are deployed in Java - data handling via collections/streams/JDBC, integration via APIs.
  • Deeplearning4j (DL4J): build and train neural networks natively on the JVM, with GPU acceleration.
  • TensorFlow Java API: load and run pre-trained TensorFlow models from Java code - train in Python, deploy in Java is a common industry split.
  • Also worth meeting: Weka (classic ML library) and the shape of an AI service call from a Java app.

jv5_13 demonstrates the ML idea in 30 honest lines: a nearest-neighbour predictor that classifies new students from examples alone - no hand-written pass/fail rule anywhere.

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
Meera: 95
Ravi: 82
scanner closed by itself

expl.en:
Java 7's try-with-resources: any object declared in the try's parentheses that implements AutoCloseable is closed automatically when the block ends - catch, crash or clean finish.

  • Compare with Unit 4: no finally needed purely for closing - the JVM writes it for you.
  • Several resources can share one try, separated by semicolons.
  • Works with files, sockets, database connections - everything closable.

title.en: Java 7 tote bag: switch on String, diamond, multi-catch

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
multi-caught: NullPointerException
[weekend!, regular day]

expl.en:
Three Java 7 conveniences in one run:

  • switch on String - before Java 7, only int-like types worked; strings needed if-else ladders.
  • Diamond operator <> - the right side borrows the element type from the left declaration.
  • Multi-catch catch (A | B e) - one handler for several unrelated exception types (no inheritance between them).

All three are compile-time conveniences the JVM never sees - but they make day-to-day Java much shorter.

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
name is String
subs is ArrayList
0: Java
1: Python
again: Java
again: Python

expl.en:
var (Java 10) tells javac: "read the type from the right side".

  • It is compile-time inference - the .class file contains the fully real type; Java stays statically typed (a var String can never later hold an int).
  • Works for local variables, counting loops and for-each - NOT for fields, parameters or return types.
  • Initialization is compulsory at declaration: var x; alone is a compile error because there is nothing to infer from.

title.en: Lambda basics: a functional interface implemented inline

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
old: I am bulky
lambda: just the body!
lambdas are values too

expl.en:
Java 8's headline feature. A functional interface has exactly ONE abstract method, so a lambda can stand in for a whole anonymous class:

  • Old style: 5 lines of anonymous-class ceremony.
  • Lambda: () -> body - parameters on the left, behaviour on the right.
  • Notice the declared type is still Speaker: the lambda IS-A Speaker; javac matches the single method by signature.
  • When the signature has no parameters, the parentheses are simply empty: () ->.

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
add: 7,3 -> 10
sub: 7,3 -> 4
mul: 7,3 -> 21
div: 2

expl.en:
When the interface's single method takes parameters, the lambda's left side lists them:

  • (x, y) -> x + y - names only; javac infers int from Calc.op's signature.
  • One-expression bodies need neither return nor braces.
  • Passing a lambda to a method (show("add:", add)) makes code behave like data - the seed of functional style.
  • Same Calc contract, four different behaviours, zero extra classes.

title.en: Lambdas with forEach: printing a list

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
--- classic for-each ---
* Meera
* Ravi
* Farhan
--- forEach + lambda ---
# Meera
# Ravi
# Farhan
shout: MEERA
shout: RAVI
shout: FARHAN

expl.en:
Syllabus: print list elements with a lambda. Every collection owns forEach(action), whose parameter type is the functional interface Consumer<T>:

  • t -> System.out.println(...) feeds each element to println, one by one.
  • Multiple statements? Wrap the body in braces, exactly like a tiny method.
  • Classic for-each vs forEach-lambda: same walk; the lambda form composes better with streams (next programs).

title.en: Practical 15 (A): filter even numbers with streams

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
all: [5, 12, 7, 20, 33, 40, 2]
--- evens only ---
* 12
* 20
* 40
* 2
even count = 4

expl.en:
Practical 15 (part A). A stream is a conveyor-belt view of a collection:

  • .stream() opens the belt; .filter(lambda) keeps only elements where the lambda returns true; .forEach(lambda) consumes each survivor.
  • The original list is never touched - streams calculate views, they do not mutate.
  • A stream is single-use: for a second pipeline (count) we open a fresh nums.stream().
  • Read it aloud: "stream, filter the evens, for each print". Almost English.

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
raw: [java, python, kotlin]
--- UPPERCASE ---
# JAVA
# PYTHON
# KOTLIN
raw is still [java, python, kotlin]

expl.en:
Practical 15 (part B). map is the transformer station on the belt: each element goes in, the lambda's result comes out.

  • map(s -> s.toUpperCase()) turns a Stream of lowercase strings into a Stream of UPPERCASE ones.
  • filter + map compose: keep only what matches, transform what survives.
  • The source list stays untouched - see it printed unchanged at the end of the run.

title.en: Stream pipeline: filter, map, sorted, collect

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
input : [88, 45, 72, 95, 61, 50]
report: [pass: 50, pass: 61, pass: 72, pass: 88, pass: 95]
passes = 5
fail: 45

expl.en:
A full pipeline reads like a query:

  • Source (stream), intermediate steps (filter, sorted, map - each returns a new stream), one terminal step (collect - pours results back into a List).
  • Intermediate steps are lazy: nothing moves until forEach/collect/count starts the belt.
  • Collectors.toList() (java.util.stream) gathers everything back into a modifiable list.
  • This is where lambdas become genuinely expressive: complete behaviour passed as parameters to a data pipeline.

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
== attendance time ==
-----------------
next period: Java lab

expl.en:
java.lang and java.util.function ship ready-made functional interfaces:

  • Runnable - void run(), classically used for threads, here simply invoked directly.
  • Supplier<T> - T get(), hands out values on demand.
  • Others in the family: Consumer<T> (accept - used by forEach), Predicate<T> (test - used by filter), Function<T,R> (apply - used by map).
  • Recognising these five names unlocks most stream code you will ever meet.

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
exam on 2027-04-20
months to go: 5
days: 23
lab at 01:30 PM
day: TUESDAY

expl.en:
Java 8 replaced the notoriously awkward Date/Calendar with java.time:

  • LocalDate / LocalTime - immutable, thread-safe, no time-zone drama.
  • Period.between() does calendar subtraction properly (months and days, not raw milliseconds).
  • Formatting via DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("hh:mm a") - the "a" prints AM/PM.
  • Run it any day: "months to go" is genuinely computed from the system clock, not hardcoded.

title.en: Records and pattern matching: exhibit + classic twin

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
7 : Meera
len = 12

expl.en:
The post-Java-8 wave keeps shrinking boilerplate:

  • record (16+): a compact immutable data class - one line writes constructor, equals, hashCode, toString and accessors (roll(), name()).
  • Pattern matching for instanceof (16+): if (o instanceof String t) tests AND binds in one breath - the cast disappears.
  • Text blocks (15+): triple-quoted multi-line strings - perfect for JSON and SQL.
  • Sealed classes (17+): a class listing exactly who may extend it.

The sandbox JDK is 11, so the commented lines show the new syntax while the classic equivalent still compiles and runs - exam answers should use the modern forms.

title.en: Mini AI: nearest-neighbour classifier in pure Java

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
k-NN verdicts:
6h/88% -> pass
1h/45% -> fail
4h/70% -> pass

expl.en:
A real (tiny) machine-learning idea running in plain Java - the spirit of "Java in AI":

  • k-Nearest-Neighbour: classify a new student by the CLOSEST known student in (hours, attendance) space - the model simply remembers examples.
  • This is what enterprise Java + DL4J do at scale: the same distance/classify loop over millions of rows, accelerated on GPUs.
  • The behaviour comes from data - change the table and the verdicts change with it. That is the definition of ML: rules derived from examples rather than hand-written ifs.

Syllabus link: meaning of AI/ML + Java's role - this program is the smallest honest demonstration of both.

q.en: What new features did Java 7 introduce?

a.en: try-with-resources, strings in switch, the diamond operator <>, and multi-catch (catch (A | B e)).

q.en: Name the headline features of Java 8.

a.en: Lambda expressions, the Stream API, java.time, and default/static methods in interfaces.

q.en: What is an LTS release? Give examples.

a.en: A Long-Term Support version industry commits to - 8, 11, 17 and 21.

q.en: What do records achieve (Java 16)?

a.en: One line declares an immutable data class: constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString all generated.

q.en: What is pattern matching for instanceof?

a.en: if (o instanceof String t) tests the type AND binds the cast variable in a single step.

q.en: What does text block syntax look like?

a.en: Triple quotes """ ... """ - multi-line strings without escape gymnastics (Java 15).

q.en: What does the try-with-resources header do?

a.en: Any AutoCloseable declared in try(...) is closed automatically on every exit path - normal, caught or crashing.

q.en: try-with-resources vs finally for closing?

a.en: finally needs hand-written null checks and close(); try-with-resources is shorter and exception-safe by construction.

q.en: What does the diamond operator do?

a.en: new ArrayList<>() infers the element type from the left-hand declaration - no repetition.

q.en: What is multi-catch used for?

a.en: One catch block for several unrelated exception types: catch (NullPointerException | ArithmeticException e).

q.en: What does var infer, and where can it be used?

a.en: The type of a local variable from its initialiser; locals and loops only - not fields, parameters or return types.

q.en: Is Java with var dynamically typed?

a.en: No - the real type is frozen at compile time into the .class; var x = "s" can never hold an int later.

q.en: What is a functional interface?

a.en: An interface with EXACTLY ONE abstract method - the unique shape a lambda can implement.

q.en: What is the lambda syntax?

a.en: (parameters) -> body. One expression needs no braces/return; multi-statements use braces.

q.en: Why can a lambda omit parameter types?

a.en: javac infers them from the single abstract method's signature - (x, y) -> x + y typed by Calc.op.

q.en: What does @FunctionalInterface do?

a.en: Asks the compiler to ERROR OUT if a second abstract method is added - protecting every lambda of that type.

q.en: Lambda vs anonymous inner class?

a.en: Same power; lambda removes the class ceremony, keeps only the interesting body - jv5_4 shows both.

q.en: Can a lambda be stored in a variable?

a.en: Yes - lambdas are values of their functional-interface type; store them, pass them, call them later.

q.en: Name four built-in functional interfaces.

a.en: Runnable (run), Supplier<T> (get), Consumer<T> (accept), Predicate<T> (test); plus Function<T,R> (apply).

q.en: Which interface powers forEach?

a.en: Consumer<T> - its accept(t) receives each element.

q.en: Write the lambda to print every team member.

a.en: team.forEach(t -> System.out.println(t));

q.en: What is a stream in Java?

a.en: A conveyor-belt VIEW over a collection: a pipeline of operations, not a storage and not a loop.

q.en: What do filter, map and forEach do?

a.en: filter keeps elements passing a Predicate; map transforms each via a Function; forEach consumes each via a Consumer.

q.en: Does a stream modify its source collection?

a.en: Never - streams compute views; the source list stays untouched (see jv5_8 output).

q.en: What does it mean that streams are lazy?

a.en: Intermediate steps (filter/map/sorted) do nothing until a terminal step (forEach/collect/count) triggers the pipeline.

q.en: Why can't you re-use a stream?

a.en: A stream is consumed once; for a second pipeline open a fresh collection.stream().

q.en: Practical 15: which two operations are demonstrated?

a.en: filter to keep even numbers, and map to convert strings to uppercase - both displayed with forEach.

q.en: What does collect(Collectors.toList()) do?

a.en: Terminal step pouring the surviving stream elements back into a new, modifiable List.

q.en: What is AI, in one exam sentence?

a.en: Machines performing tasks that normally require human intelligence - recognition, decisions, prediction, language.

q.en: What is Machine Learning?

a.en: Programs that learn their behaviour from DATA/examples rather than hand-written rules - change the data, change the behaviour.

q.en: How does Deep Learning fit inside AI?

a.en: DL is a branch of ML using layered neural networks; ML is inside AI; classic rule-based AI needs no learning.

q.en: Contrast a rule-based program with an ML one.

a.en: Rules: if mark < 33 then fail (hand-written). ML: like jv5_13 - verdict comes from the most similar past example.

q.en: What is the role of Java in AI?

a.en: Java runs the enterprise backends where AI features get deployed: strong data handling (collections/streams/JDBC) and API integration at scale.

q.en: Name two AI libraries for Java.

a.en: Deeplearning4j (train and run neural nets on the JVM) and TensorFlow Java API (run pre-trained TF models from Java).

q.en: What is Deeplearning4j used for?

a.en: Building and training neural networks natively in Java/JVM languages, with GPU acceleration - the Java answer to deep learning.

q.en: What is TensorFlow Java API used for?

a.en: Loading pre-trained TensorFlow models and scoring them from Java code - the 'deploy in Java' half of a Python-training workflow.

q.en: What does k-NN do? (jv5_13)

a.en: Classifies a new case by the CLOSEST stored example - predicting pass/fail from hours-studied and attendance without any if-rule.

q.en: Why is jv5_13 genuinely ML and not just if-else?

a.en: Because its verdicts are derived from the example table: edit the data and the answers change - behaviour learned, not coded.

q.en: What is the industry split between Python and Java AI?

a.en: Python typically TRAINS models; Java DEPLOYS them inside large-scale services.

q.en: Mention two more post-8 conveniences students should recognise.

a.en: switch expressions with arrow labels (Java 14) and sealed classes (Java 17) - listed for theory; run on later JDKs.

q.en: Which Java feature makes Scanner/file closing safest, and since when?

a.en: try-with-resources, since Java 7.
